sections.title: Introduction
sections.question: Why smooth values on a graph?
sections.answer: Neighbouring nodes should have similar values.
sections.sell: Sets the question: values on neighbouring nodes should agree.
sections.lead: This survey asks why values on a graph should be smoothed. Nothing is assumed yet; the next section gives the operation that does it.
sections.bridge: Section 2 defines the averaging step used throughout.
glossary: Replacing each node's value by something closer to its neighbours'. It removes noise that varies quickly between neighbours, at the price of blurring real sharp edges, so the amount of smoothing is a trade-off to choose.

claims.text: The weighted average minimises $\sum_i w_i\|x_i-c\|^2$ over $c$.

sections.title: Neighbour averaging
sections.question: How does repeated averaging smooth?
sections.answer: Each step replaces a value by its neighbours' mean; high frequencies decay fastest.
sections.sell: One averaging step is a matrix-vector product; repeating it damps high frequencies.

concepts.name: weighted average $\bar x_w$
concepts.gist: A mean in which some points count more than others; it is how the toy method lets near points speak louder than far ones.
concepts.explain: With weights $w_i\ge0$ summing to 1, the weighted average moves toward the heavily weighted points. In the toy method the weights come from distance, so a point's smoothed value is dominated by its neighbours; this is what removes noise that changes quickly from one neighbour to the next. A common slip is to forget to divide by the sum of the weights, which silently rescales the result.
